f.title: Treat only persistent or significant disability as serious, not minor events
f.statement: Only a persistent or significant or incapacitating disability is intended in the definition of serious. Disability is not intended to include experiences of relatively minor medical significance such as headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, influenza and accidental trauma (e.g., sprained ankle).

disability that would constitute a serious adverse drug experience is 
also described in the final ICH E2A guideline, which states that a 
serious adverse drug experience is based on events that pose a threat 
to a patient's life or functioning and not on events of relatively 
minor medical significance (60 FR 11284 at 11285). Thus, disability is

f.title: Submit initial written IND safety reports within 15 days once the minimum criteria are met
f.statement: Sponsors are advised, as described in the ICH E2A guideline, to submit as much information as possible on a case in written IND safety reports. Where information for final description and evaluation is not available within 15 calendar days, initial reports should nevertheless be submitted within this timeframe when the minimum criteria are met: an identifiable patient; a suspected medicinal product; an identifiable reporter; and an adverse event or outcome that can be identified as serious and unexpected and for which, in clinical investigation cases, there is a reasonable suspected causal relationship (the causal relationship cannot be ruled out).

f.statement: For 21 CFR 310.305: A serious adverse drug experience is one occurring at any dose that results in death, a life-threatening adverse drug experience, inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, a persistent or significant disability/incapacity, or a congenital anomaly/birth defect. f.title: Apply the unexpected definition for postmarketing reporting (310.305(b))
f.statement: For 21 CFR 310.305: An unexpected adverse drug experience is one not listed in the current labeling for the drug product, including events symptomatically and pathophysiologically related to a labeled event but differing from it by greater severity or specificity (e.g., hepatic necrosis when labeling refers only to elevated hepatic enzymes or hepatitis; cerebral thromboembolism or cerebral vasculitis when labeling lists only cerebral vascular accidents). "Unexpected" in this definition refers to an adverse drug experience that has not been previously observed (i.e., included in the labeling), rather than to whether the experience could be anticipated from the pharmacological properties of the pharmaceutical product.

f.title: Apply the serious definition for postmarketing reporting (314.80(a))
f.statement: For 21 CFR 314.80: A serious adverse drug experience is one occurring at any dose that results in death, a life-threatening adverse drug experience, inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, a persistent or significant disability/incapacity, or a congenital anomaly/birth defect. Important medical events that may not result in death, be life-threatening or require hospitalization may be considered serious when, based on appropriate medical judgment, they may jeopardize the patient or subject and may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of those outcomes (examples: allergic bronchospasm requiring intensive treatment in an emergency room or at home, blood dyscrasias or convulsions not resulting in inpatient hospitalization, development of drug dependency or drug abuse).

f.title: Apply the unexpected definition for postmarketing reporting (314.80(a))
f.statement: For 21 CFR 314.80: An unexpected adverse drug experience is one not listed in the current labeling for the drug product, including events symptomatically and pathophysiologically related to a labeled event but differing from it by greater severity or specificity (e.g., hepatic necrosis when labeling refers only to elevated hepatic enzymes or hepatitis; cerebral thromboembolism or cerebral vasculitis when labeling lists only cerebral vascular accidents). "Unexpected" in this definition refers to an adverse drug experience that has not been previously observed (i.e., included in the labeling), rather than to whether the experience could be anticipated from the pharmacological properties of the pharmaceutical product.
f.applicability: Drugs with approved applications under 21 CFR part 314 (21 CFR 314.80). Text as amended by the 1997 final rule (effective April 6, 1998). These postmarketing sections may have been amended by later rulemaking (for example the June 10, 2014 final rule on electronic submission of postmarketing safety reports), so check the current CFR.

rows.quote:
Unexpected adverse drug experience. Any adverse drug experience 
that is not listed in the current labeling for the drug product. This 
includes events that may be symptomatically and pathophysiologically 
related to an event listed in the labeling, but differ from the event 
because of greater severity or specificity. For example, under this 
definition, hepatic necrosis would be unexpected (by virtue of greater 
severity) if the labeling only referred to elevated hepatic enzymes or 
hepatitis. Similarly, cerebral thromboembolism and cerebral vasculitis 
would be unexpected (by virtue of greater specificity) if the labeling 
only listed cerebral vascular accidents. ``Unexpected,'' as used in 
this definition, refers to an adverse drug experience that has not been 
previously observed (i.e., included in the labeling) rather than from 
the perspective of such experience not being anticipated from the 
pharmacological properties of the pharmaceutical product.

f.title: Assess expectedness against current labeling for biological products (600.80)
f.statement: For 21 CFR 600.80, an unexpected adverse experience is one not listed in the current labeling for the biological product, including events symptomatically and pathophysiologically related to a labeled event but differing by greater severity or specificity (e.g., hepatic necrosis when labeling refers only to elevated hepatic enzymes or hepatitis; cerebral thromboembolism or cerebral vasculitis when labeling lists only cerebral vascular accidents). For 21 CFR 600.80, "unexpected" refers to an adverse experience that has not been previously observed (i.e., included in the labeling), rather than to whether it could be anticipated from the pharmacological properties of the pharmaceutical product.

rows.quote:
Unexpected adverse experience: Any adverse experience that is not 
listed in the current labeling for the biological product. This 
includes events that may be symptomatically and pathophysiologically 
related to an event listed in the labeling, but differ from the event 
because of greater severity or specificity. For example, under this 
definition, hepatic necrosis would be unexpected (by virtue of greater 
severity) if the labeling only referred to elevated hepatic enzymes or 
hepatitis. Similarly, cerebral thromboembolism and cerebral vasculitis 
would be unexpected (by virtue of greater specificity) if the labeling 
only listed cerebral vascular accidents. ``Unexpected,'' as used in

previously observed (i.e., included in the labeling) rather than from
